framework.name: NIST CSF
framework.summary: Voluntary US framework from NIST for managing cybersecurity risk, used by organisations worldwide. US regulators, customers and insurers often ask for it. Its Core lists 106 outcomes across six functions, from governing to recovering.

groups.title: Identity management, authentication and access control

requirements.title: Security decisions start from what the organisation exists to deliver.
The organisation knows who has a stake in its security and what each expects.
Security and privacy duties from law, regulation and contracts are known and met.
The services others rely on the organisation for are known and made clear to them.
The services and suppliers the organisation itself relies on are known and made clear.
Leadership and other stakeholders have agreed what managing security risk should achieve.
Leadership has written down how much risk it accepts, and keeps that statement current.
Security risk is handled as part of the organisation's overall business risk management.
Leadership has said which ways of responding to risk are preferred, and staff know them.
Everyone knows how to raise security risks, including those coming from suppliers.
Security risks are scored, recorded and ranked with one shared method everyone knows.
Risk discussions also weigh the chances that security work opens up for the business.
Leadership owns security risk and leads a culture that is alert to risk, ethical and improving.
Every security role has clear duties and authority that people understand and follow.
The security programme gets the people, money and tools its strategy actually needs.
Hiring, onboarding, role changes and departures all take security into account.
Security policy fits the organisation's situation and priorities, is shared and is enforced.
Security policy is revised whenever duties, threats, technology or the mission change.
Leadership looks at what the security strategy has achieved and changes course where needed.
The security strategy is checked regularly to make sure it still covers every risk and duty.
How well security risk is being managed is measured and reviewed for needed changes.
There is an agreed programme, with goals and rules, for managing supplier security risk.
Suppliers, customers and partners know which security tasks are theirs and which are yours.
Supplier risk is weighed in the same risk assessments and improvement work as other risks.
Every supplier is known and ranked by how much the organisation depends on it.
Security expectations for suppliers are set by priority and written into their contracts.
A new supplier's security is checked and planned for before anything is signed.
Each supplier's risks are assessed, logged, acted on and monitored throughout the relationship.
Key suppliers have a part in planning for, handling and recovering from incidents.
Supplier security is part of risk management and tracked over each product's whole life.
Plans cover what must happen with access, data and duties when a supplier relationship ends.
There is an up-to-date list of the hardware the organisation manages.
There is an up-to-date list of the software, services and systems the organisation runs.
Current maps show which network connections and data flows are allowed, inside and out.
There is an up-to-date list of the services each supplier provides.
Assets are ranked by sensitivity, criticality and the harm their loss would cause.
Important kinds of data are listed, together with where they live and who owns them.
Systems, devices, software, services and data are looked after from purchase to disposal.
Weaknesses in systems and devices are found, confirmed and logged.
Warnings about cyber threats arrive regularly from trusted sharing groups and sources.
A written list names who or what could attack or harm the organisation, inside or out.
The likelihood and harm of each threat exploiting a weakness are recorded.
Threats, weaknesses, likelihood and impact together decide which risks get dealt with first.
For each risk a response is chosen, planned, followed through and reported.
System changes and policy exceptions are risk-assessed, recorded and tracked.
Outsiders can report security flaws, and the reports are assessed and acted on.
Hardware and software are checked to be genuine and untampered before they are bought or used.
Critical suppliers are assessed for security before the organisation commits to buying from them.
Audits, reviews and other assessments lead to concrete improvements.
Security tests and exercises, including those run with suppliers, lead to concrete improvements.
Lessons from running day-to-day processes and procedures lead to better ways of working.
Incident plans, and any security plan that shapes daily operations, are shared, kept current and improved.
Every authorised person, service and device has a managed identity and credentials.
People prove who they are before receiving credentials, to a degree that matches the risk.
People, services and devices must prove their identity before they get access.
Sign-in tokens and other proofs of identity are protected in transit and checked on receipt.
Access rights follow written rules, are kept minimal and split, and are reviewed regularly.
Physical access to sites and equipment is controlled and watched in line with the risk.
Everyone gets the security awareness and training needed to do their everyday work safely.
People in specialist roles get the extra security training their tasks demand.
Stored data cannot be read, changed or made unavailable by anyone unauthorised.
Data moving across networks cannot be read, altered or blocked by anyone unauthorised.
Data being processed in memory cannot be read, altered or disrupted by anyone unauthorised.
Backups are made, protected, kept current and tested by restoring from them.
Systems are set up from approved configurations, and changes to those settings are controlled.
Software is updated, replaced or removed in good time according to its risk.
Hardware is serviced, replaced or disposed of in good time according to its risk.
Systems produce activity logs that are available for ongoing monitoring.
Software that has not been approved cannot be installed or run.
Software is built with secure practices at every stage, and how well they work is checked.
Networks and system environments are shielded from unauthorised access and use.
Technology is protected from fire, flood, power loss and other environmental hazards.
Systems are built to keep working as required in both normal times and crises.
There is enough capacity in systems and networks to keep services available.
Someone keeps watch on network traffic and services to catch attacks or misuse early.
Buildings and rooms are watched for intrusions and other physical incidents.
User activity and the use of technology are watched for signs of trouble.
The activity and services of outside providers are watched for signs of trouble.
Computers, applications and the platforms they run on are watched for signs of compromise.
Suspicious events are examined to work out what activity lies behind them.
Information from several sources is brought together to reveal connected events.
The likely impact and reach of a suspicious event are worked out.
Details of suspicious events reach the authorised people and tools that need them.
Threat intelligence and business context are used when analysing suspicious events.
An incident is declared whenever events meet the criteria agreed in advance.
A declared incident triggers the agreed response plan, working alongside outside helpers where needed.
Incoming incident reports are sorted and checked to confirm they are real.
Each incident is sorted by type and ranked by urgency.
Incidents are passed up to more senior people or specialists when needed.
Agreed criteria decide when the response moves on to recovery.
Investigators establish what happened during an incident and why it happened.
Every step of an investigation is logged in a way that proves the record is genuine.
Data about an incident is gathered and kept so its origin and integrity can be proven.
How large an incident is gets estimated and then confirmed.
The people inside and outside the organisation who must know about an incident are told.
Incident information is shared with the internal and external parties agreed in advance.
Incidents are stopped from spreading further.
The cause of an incident, such as malware or attacker access, is removed.
Recovery work begins as planned once the incident team hands over to it.
Recovery steps are chosen, scoped, put in order and carried out.
Backups and other restore sources are checked to be intact before they are used.
After an incident, critical business functions and security needs shape the new normal.
Restored systems are checked to be intact and working before normal service is confirmed.
Recovery is declared finished against agreed criteria, and its records are completed.
Staff, customers and other agreed contacts hear how far service restoration has got.
Only agreed spokespeople and pre-approved wording are used when telling the public how recovery is going.
